title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
extended_summary:
This paper examines how features of Learning Assistant (LA)-supported undergraduate STEM courses are associated with student learning outcomes. The authors use pilot data from a multi-institution study to ask whether student characteristics, instructor experience, course features, and the amount of interaction with LAs predict gains on concept inventories.

The intervention/approach studied is the Learning Assistant model, in which undergraduate or course-embedded assistants support instruction in STEM classes. Data were collected from faculty surveys and student pre/post concept inventory surveys across several institutions in the LA Alliance. The sample includes physics, biology, and chemistry courses, with outcomes measured using standardized concept inventories and effect sizes based on pre/post score changes.

The study reports that average learning gains were positive overall, with larger gains associated with more student interaction with LAs, more faculty experience teaching the course with LAs, and better student-to-LA ratios. However, the findings also show gender and race-related differences in outcomes, with male students outperforming female students and some racial groups differing from White students. The authors emphasize that these are correlational findings from preliminary data and that future work is needed to disentangle causal effects and examine specific LA practices more closely.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational multi-site study using hierarchical linear models, but it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental design and does not identify causal effects of a technology intervention. The evidence is useful for pattern detection and hypothesis generation, but credibility for impact claims is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports moderate pre-post gains in concept inventory outcomes, but these are not attributable to a specific AI/technology intervention and are highly context-dependent. It therefore suggests unclear to modest impact rather than a clearly demonstrated intervention effect.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational HLM study of LA-supported STEM courses found overall pre-post gains in concept inventories, with a grand mean effect size of d=0.845 across 3,315 usable student pre/post pairs. However, outcomes varied substantially by discipline and student subgroup, and the paper does not isolate a causal effect of the Learning Assistant model itself.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory effect sizes (Cohen's d) on FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, CCI, and GCIICS
finding.study_size: n=3,315 usable pre-post pairs; 17 instructors; 13 institutions
finding.effect_size: d=0.845 overall; by inventory ranged from d=0.052 (CCI) to d=1.248 (CINS)

finding.finding_summary: Student interaction time with LAs was positively associated with learning gains, peaking for students who spent 16-30 minutes per week with LAs. Compared with the 0 min/week group (d=0.369), the 16-30 min/week group had substantially higher average effect size (d=0.873), while the 30+ min/week group showed no further increase, suggesting a possible selection effect among the most struggling students.
finding.measure: Weekly minutes of student interaction with Learning Assistants and resulting concept inventory effect sizes
finding.effect_size: d=0.873 for 16-30 min/week vs d=0.369 for 0 min/week

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students in courses with more experienced LA-using instructors had higher learning gains, with effect size increasing by 0.154 for each additional term a faculty member had taught the course with LAs. More faculty co-planning time with LAs was also associated with better performance (+0.004 effect size per additional minute/week), although this relationship was not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Instructor experience teaching with LAs; faculty meeting/co-planning time with LAs; student concept inventory effect sizes
finding.effect_size: +0.154 per additional term taught with LAs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports institutional and classroom-level variation in LA-supported outcomes, suggesting that implementation context matters for scalability and best-practice development. At the same time, the authors identify inequitable patterns by gender and race, including lower average effect sizes for female students (d=0.485) than male students (d=0.749), indicating that the LA model did not eliminate existing disparities in these settings.
finding.measure: Student concept inventory effect sizes disaggregated by gender and race; course/institution context features
finding.study_size: n=3,315 usable pre-post pairs; 17 instructors; 13 institutions
finding.effect_size: Female d=0.485 vs male d=0.749; white d=0.619 vs Asian d=0.557 and other d=0.509
